    The route to membership

    The current scheme has three academic levels, four self-paced modules and two years of practical training. Your exact route depends on whether you enter through Foundation or Direct Entry.

    01

    Foundation

    Four papers. Start after Class 10 registration and appear after Class 12 plus the required four-month study period.

    →
    02

    Intermediate

    Six papers in two groups. Foundation pass or Direct Entry for eligible graduates and ICSI/ICMAI intermediate-level candidates.

    →
    03

    Final + training

    Six papers, four SPOM sets, ICITSS/AICITSS and two years of practical training complete the academic-professional pathway.

    !
    Direct Entry is not a shortcut through Intermediate. Commerce graduates/post-graduates need at least 55%; other graduates/post-graduates need at least 60%. An eight-month Intermediate study period still applies.

    Study library: the core ideas in one place

    These compact notes cover the concepts and formulas that recur across CA papers. Use the search and level filters, then test yourself in the worked questions below.

    Foundation · Accounting

    Accounting mechanics

    • Every transaction preserves the equation: Assets = Equity + Liabilities.
    • Debit increases assets/expenses; credit increases capital, liabilities and income.
    • A trial balance checks arithmetic equality, not complete accuracy: omission and principle errors may remain.
    • Depreciable amount is cost less residual value; match the method to the asset's consumption pattern.
    SLM depreciation = (Cost − Residual value) ÷ Useful life
    Foundation · Business Laws

    Contract answer framework

    • A valid agreement needs competent parties, free consent, lawful consideration and lawful object.
    • An offer must be communicated; acceptance must be absolute and correspond to the offer.
    • Distinguish void, voidable, illegal and unenforceable agreements before discussing remedy.
    • Write answers as Issue → Rule → Apply facts → Conclusion.
    Foundation · Business Mathematics

    Time value and ratios

    • Keep rate and time in the same period before using an interest formula.
    • A ratio compares like quantities; a proportion states equality of two ratios.
    • For annuities, identify whether cash flow occurs at the end or beginning of each period.
    Amount (compound) = P(1 + r)ⁿ · PV = FV ÷ (1 + r)ⁿ
    Foundation · Statistics

    Central tendency and spread

    • Mean uses every value but is sensitive to extremes; median is positional and robust to extremes.
    • Variance is the mean squared deviation; standard deviation restores the original unit.
    • Correlation measures association, not causation. Its coefficient lies between −1 and +1.
    σ = √[Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ N] · CV = (σ ÷ x̄) × 100
    Foundation · Economics

    Demand, supply and elasticity

    • A movement along demand follows own-price change; a shift follows income, tastes, expectations or related-goods prices.
    • Elastic demand has |Ed| > 1; inelastic demand has |Ed| < 1.
    • Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative forgone.
    • Marginal thinking compares the extra benefit and extra cost of one more unit.
    Price elasticity of demand = %Δ quantity demanded ÷ %Δ price
    Intermediate · Advanced Accounting

    Standard-led problem solving

    • Start by identifying the recognition question, measurement basis and presentation/disclosure impact.
    • Inventory is generally carried at the lower of cost and net realisable value.
    • Cash flow classification separates operating, investing and financing activities.
    • Show adjustment entries and working notes before the final statement.
    NRV = Estimated selling price − Completion cost − Selling cost
    Intermediate · Corporate & Other Laws

    Provision-to-facts method

    • First identify entity, actor, power, condition, time limit and consequence.
    • Separate the general rule from exceptions and provisos.
    • Do not invent section numbers; accurate principle and application beat a wrong citation.
    • Conclude only after applying each decisive fact to the rule.
    Intermediate · Taxation

    Tax computation discipline

    • Income-tax flow: scope → residential status → heads of income → set-off → deductions → tax liability.
    • GST flow: supply → time → place → value → rate → input tax credit → net liability.
    • Build a separate amendment sheet for the exact attempt; never mix assessment years.
    • State assumptions when facts are incomplete.
    Net GST payable = Output tax liability − Eligible input tax credit
    Intermediate · Costing

    Decision formulas

    • Contribution first covers fixed cost; the remainder is profit.
    • Relevant cost changes between alternatives and relates to the future.
    • Standard costing separates price/rate effects from quantity/efficiency effects.
    • Reconcile cost and financial profits systematically, not from memory.
    Contribution = Sales − Variable cost · P/V ratio = Contribution ÷ Sales · BEP sales = Fixed cost ÷ P/V ratio
    Intermediate · Auditing & Ethics

    Risk and evidence

    • Management assertions guide procedures: existence, completeness, rights/obligations, valuation and presentation.
    • Audit evidence must be sufficient (quantity) and appropriate (quality).
    • Professional scepticism means a questioning mind and alertness to contradiction.
    • Link procedure to risk: inspect, observe, confirm, recalculate, reperform, inquire or analyse.
    Audit risk = Inherent risk × Control risk × Detection risk
    Intermediate · FM & Strategy

    Value and strategic fit

    • Accept a conventional project when NPV is positive at the required return, subject to constraints and qualitative factors.
    • WACC uses market-value weights where appropriate and an after-tax cost of debt.
    • Strategy links external opportunity/threat with internal strength/weakness and execution capability.
    • A ratio is a prompt for investigation, not a conclusion by itself.
    NPV = Σ[Cash flowₜ ÷ (1+k)ᵗ] − Initial outlay
    Final · Financial Reporting

    Recognition before calculation

    • Identify control, significant influence or a simple financial-asset relationship before choosing accounting treatment.
    • For financial instruments, classification drives subsequent measurement and impairment treatment.
    • Revenue analysis starts with contract, performance obligations and timing of satisfaction.
    • In consolidation, eliminate intragroup balances and unrealised profits consistently.
    Final · Advanced FM

    Valuation and risk

    • Discount cash flows matching the claim: FCFF with WACC, FCFE with cost of equity.
    • A hedge reduces exposure; it does not need to create a speculative gain.
    • Separate operating synergy from financing effects in acquisition valuation.
    • State quotation convention and timeline before a forex calculation.
    FCFF = EBIT(1−T) + Depreciation − Capex − ΔWorking capital
    Final · Advanced Audit

    Report from evidence

    • Move from identified risk to response, evidence, conclusion and reporting implication.
    • Material misstatement can arise from error or fraud; fraud adds incentives, opportunity and rationalisation concerns.
    • Going concern assessment and auditor reporting are related but distinct decisions.
    • Ethics answers should identify threat, significance, safeguards and whether the engagement can continue.
    Final · Direct & International Tax

    Cross-border framework

    • Classify the taxpayer and transaction before applying domestic charging provisions.
    • Then test treaty access, permanent establishment and allocation rules where relevant.
    • Transfer pricing focuses on the arm's-length outcome between associated enterprises.
    • Document assumptions and apply only provisions relevant to the notified attempt.
    Final · Indirect Tax

    Transaction map

    • Resolve classification and supply first; valuation and rate follow that answer.
    • Time of supply identifies when liability arises; place of supply helps determine tax type and jurisdiction.
    • Input tax credit requires eligibility, documentation and absence of a blocked-credit rule.
    • Customs problems need assessable value, exchange-rate/date rules and the correct duty sequence.
    Final · Integrated Business Solutions

    Open-book case method

    • Build a slim topic index before the exam; searching from scratch consumes time.
    • Read the requirement before the case, then tag facts by finance, tax, law, risk and strategy.
    • Prioritise recommendation and reasoning over copying theory.
    • State commercial trade-offs, assumptions and implementation risks.
    Final · SPOM

    Four modules, four qualifications

    • Set A: Corporate & Economic Laws; Set B: Strategic Cost & Performance Management.
    • Set C: choose one elective; Set D: choose one multidisciplinary subject.
    • Finish required learning hours before the module test.
    • Treat SPOMs as part of Final eligibility, not as a post-exam formality.

    Practice with explanations

    Try each question on paper before opening the answer. The explanation shows the reasoning—not just the result.

    1. A machine costs ₹5,00,000, has a ₹50,000 residual value and a 5-year useful life. What is annual straight-line depreciation?
    ₹90,000. Depreciable amount = ₹5,00,000 − ₹50,000 = ₹4,50,000. Divide by five years: ₹90,000 per year.
    2. Why can a trial balance agree even when the accounts contain an error?
    Because it tests debit-credit equality, not complete correctness. A complete omission, an equal error on both sides, or posting to the wrong account of the same type can leave total debits equal to total credits.
    3. Price rises by 10% and quantity demanded falls by 20%. What is the magnitude of price elasticity?
    2, so demand is elastic. |Ed| = 20% ÷ 10% = 2. The negative direction is understood from the law of demand; classification usually uses the magnitude.
    4. A product sells for ₹500 with variable cost of ₹300. Fixed cost is ₹4,00,000. What is the break-even volume?
    2,000 units. Contribution per unit = ₹500 − ₹300 = ₹200. Break-even units = ₹4,00,000 ÷ ₹200.
    5. What is the strongest first step in a business-law case answer?
    Identify the legal issue from the facts. Then state the applicable rule, apply decisive facts and conclude. Starting with unrelated theory wastes time and can obscure the issue.
    6. If output GST is ₹1,20,000 and eligible input tax credit is ₹85,000, what is the simple net liability before interest or other adjustments?
    ₹35,000. Net liability = output tax liability − eligible input tax credit. Eligibility must be tested before taking the credit.
    7. What makes audit evidence “appropriate”?
    Its relevance and reliability. Sufficiency refers to quantity. Appropriateness refers to quality—whether the evidence supports the assertion and how dependable its source and nature are.
    8. A project costs ₹1,00,000 and the present value of expected cash inflows is ₹1,18,000. What is its NPV and basic decision?
    NPV is ₹18,000; accept in the basic unconstrained case. NPV = ₹1,18,000 − ₹1,00,000. A positive NPV indicates value above the required return, though constraints and non-financial risks still matter.
    9. Why should FCFF normally be discounted at WACC rather than only the cost of equity?
    FCFF belongs to all capital providers. WACC reflects the required returns of debt and equity in their capital weights. FCFE, which belongs only to equity holders, is discounted at cost of equity.
    10. In an open-book case paper, why is a prepared index more valuable than carrying more material?
    Because retrieval time is the constraint. A compact index turns material into usable evidence quickly; unindexed volumes can consume the time needed for analysis and writing.
    11. What is the minimum pass rule common to Foundation and to each Intermediate/Final group?
    At least 40% in each paper and 50% in aggregate. Intermediate and Final also contain group-specific rules and exemptions, so verify your exact situation in ICAI's current FAQ.
    12. A student scored 60% in an Intermediate paper but did not pass the group. What should they check?
    Whether the ICAI paper exemption applies. Under the current FAQ, 60% or more can create an exemption for the next three examinations when the student appeared in all papers of the group; aggregate requirements still apply.

    A study loop that survives a long course

    CA preparation improves when every chapter moves through the same four passes. Watching a class is only the first pass.

    01

    Learn

    Read the ICAI chapter and class notes. Mark illustrations, provisions, formats and exceptions—not entire pages.

    02

    Recall

    Close the book. Rebuild the formula, provision, audit procedure or answer skeleton from memory.

    03

    Apply

    Solve ICAI illustrations, module questions, MCQs and past questions. Maintain one error log.

    04

    Simulate

    Write timed sectional tests, then full MTP/RTP-style papers. Review presentation and unfinished questions.

    90 minPrimary subject: new concept + two worked examples
    60 minPractice: questions without watching solutions first
    45 minSecond subject: law/audit/economics active recall
    30 minRevision: yesterday + 7-day-old topics
    15 minError log: record why the mistake happened and the correction rule

    Weekly non-negotiables

    • ✓One cumulative test under a fixed timer
    • ✓One amendment/applicability check for tax and law
    • ✓One written-answer review for structure and keywords
    • ✓One backlog decision: schedule, shrink or drop
    • ✓One half-day with no new content—revision only

    The 12-week revision sprint

    Use this after first coverage. If your preparation window is longer, repeat the first four-week block by subject before entering testing mode.

    Weeks 1–4

    Close conceptual gaps

    Map every chapter as green, amber or red. Relearn red chapters from ICAI material; solve representative questions immediately.

    Weeks 5–8

    Convert coverage into recall

    Run mixed chapter tests, compress notes, revisit the error log and practise provisions/formulas without prompts.

    Weeks 9–10

    Full-paper simulation

    Alternate full papers and review days. Track attempted marks, time leakage, presentation and avoidable errors.

    Week 11

    Patch weak zones

    Use test evidence—not anxiety—to choose chapters. Redo incorrect questions and rehearse high-frequency formats.

    Week 12

    Stabilise, don't expand

    Revision notes, amendments, key illustrations and one light simulation. No new teacher, book or question bank.

    Every Sunday

    Audit the system

    Compare planned versus completed hours, update the next seven days, and protect sleep before adding workload.

    Build today's study block

    Choose your level and available time. The planner creates a balanced session you can copy or download. It does not save personal data.

    Complete Study Material

    Ten full-syllabus chapters — CA Foundation Accounting, Business Laws, Quantitative Aptitude and Business Economics, plus Inter-level Income Tax and companion topics. Read a chapter, then test yourself in the MCQ section below.

    Exam-day rule: statutory thresholds, tax figures and amendment-driven points carry a verify against current ICAI material highlight. Rules and limits change between attempts — always cross-check the current attempt's ICAI modules, RTP and bare Acts before relying on a figure.
    Accounting: Journal, Ledger &amp; Trial Balance Partnership, Company &amp; Cash Flow Accounts Business Laws (Contract Act, Sale of Goods, LLP, Companies Act 2013) Quantitative Aptitude (Interest, Ratios, Statistics, Probability) Business Economics (Micro &amp; Macro) Income Tax: Heads of Income, Deductions &amp; Computation Basics GST: Levy, Input Tax Credit &amp; Returns Basics Auditing: Standards, Evidence &amp; Company Audit Financial Management: Ratios, Leverage &amp; Capital Budgeting Business Correspondence, Ethics &amp; Communication

    1. Accounting: Journal, Ledger & Trial Balance

    Every rupee that moves through a business leaves two footprints — one debit and one credit. The entire accounting cycle of the CA Foundation paper rests on this duality: Journal records transactions in chronological order, the Ledger classifies them account-wise, and the Trial Balance tests the arithmetic of the whole exercise.

    The golden rules (traditional classification)

    • Personal accounts (persons, firms, debtors/creditors): Debit the receiver, credit the giver.
    • Real accounts (assets — tangible and intangible): Debit what comes in, credit what goes out.
    • Nominal accounts (incomes, expenses, gains, losses): Debit all expenses and losses, credit all incomes and gains.

    The modern approach gives the same answers through five heads: assets, liabilities, capital, income, expenses — an increase in an asset or expense is a debit; an increase in a liability, capital, or income is a credit. In the exam, use whichever lens you are fastest with, but stay consistent inside one solution.

    Journal entry anatomy

    A journal entry always contains: date, account debited (written first, at the margin), account credited (indented, preceded by "To"), narration in brackets, and the ledger folio (L.F.). Format:

    • Cash A/c ——— Dr 50,000
          To Capital A/c 50,000
      (Being capital introduced into the business)

    Watch the traps: discount allowed is an expense (debit), discount received is a gain (credit). Purchases and sales of goods are nominal-ish merchandise accounts; a cash purchase is Purchases A/c Dr / To Cash A/c, never "Cash A/c Dr / To Purchases". Drawings reduce capital — Drawings A/c Dr / To Cash A/c; goods taken for personal use are credited to Purchases (goods given away), not Sales.

    From journal to ledger

    Posting transfers each journal line to its ledger account — debits to the debit side, credits to the credit side, with the journal folio (J.F.) cross-referenced. Accounts are then balanced: total both sides, carry the difference as "Balance c/d" on the shorter side, bring it down as "Balance b/d". A debit balance sits on assets/expenses; a credit balance on liabilities/incomes.

    Trial Balance — what it proves and what it hides

    The Trial Balance lists all ledger balances at a date; if total debits equal total credits, the double entry is arithmetically intact. That is all it proves. These errors do not disturb the Trial Balance: complete omission of a transaction, compensating errors, errors of principle (e.g., debited machinery repairs to the Machinery account), wrong amounts in both legs, and entries posted to the wrong account of the correct class. One-sided errors (posting a wrong amount, omitting one leg, double posting) make the totals disagree — the difference is parked in a Suspense Account until rectified.

    Subsidiary books and rectification

    Before the journal, transactions pass through subsidiary books: Purchases Book, Sales Book, Returns Books, Bills Receivable/Payable Books, and the Cash Book (single, double, and triple column — the triple-column cash book with discount, cash, and bank columns acts as both journal and ledger for cash). Petty cash uses the imprest system. A Bank Reconciliation Statement reconciles the cash book balance with the pass book: add cheques issued but not presented and uncredited items per the pass book side, subtract cheques deposited but not cleared — start from the balance you have and adjust for the timing differences, never both ways.

    Rectification of errors

    Two-sided errors (wrong account, wrong principle, complete omission from one leg's counterpart) are fixed by a corrective journal entry. One-sided errors are corrected by debiting/crediting the affected account with a corresponding entry through the Suspense Account — e.g., sales of ₹5,000 posted as ₹500 to the Sales Account: Suspense A/c Dr 4,500 / To Sales A/c 4,500. If the Trial Balance disagrees and the error is undiscovered, the Suspense Account carries the difference temporarily and is closed once rectified — it must never appear in final accounts.

    Common exam traps

    • Trial Balance totals agree ≠ books are correct. Say this explicitly when asked.
    • Suspense Account appears on the Trial Balance only as a plug; it must be closed by rectification entries, never carried to final accounts.
    • Goods distributed as free samples: Advertisement/ Free Samples A/c Dr / To Purchases A/c — not Sales.
    • Bad debts recovered: Cash A/c Dr / To Bad Debts Recovered A/c (income), not a reduction of the old debtor.

    2. Partnership, Company & Cash Flow Accounts

    These three topics dominate the accounting paper's long questions. Each has a fixed skeleton — learn the skeleton first, then the numbers fall in.

    Partnership accounts

    Governed by the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 (verify against latest ICAI material for any amended figures). Absent an agreement, the default rules apply: profits shared equally, no interest on capital, no salary/commission to partners, and 6% p.a. interest on loans/advances by a partner. With an agreement, the Profit & Loss Appropriation Account is the workhorse: net profit is appropriated as interest on capital, partner salaries/commission, and residual profit in the profit-sharing ratio — appropriations can never exceed available profits.

    • Fixed vs fluctuating capital: under fixed capital, all adjustments (interest, salary, drawings) go through Current Accounts; under fluctuating capital, straight into the Capital Accounts.
    • Interest on drawings: charged at the agreed rate; drawings at the beginning of each month use the average period of 6.5 months, middle 6 months, end 5.5 months (for monthly drawings over a year).
    • Guarantee of minimum profit: shortfall to the guaranteed partner is borne by the guaranteeing partner(s) in their agreed ratio.

    Admission of a partner triggers: new profit-sharing ratio and sacrificing ratio (old − new), revaluation of assets/liabilities (Revaluation A/c; profit/loss to old partners in the old ratio), adjustment for reserves and accumulated profits (to old partners), goodwill treatment, and capital adjustments. Retirement/death mirrors this: gaining ratio (new − old) governs goodwill adjustments; the retiring partner's share of revaluation profit and reserves is credited to them; the amount due is transferred to a Loan Account if not paid immediately. On death, profit up to the date of death is estimated on a time or turnover basis.

    Company accounts

    Share issue mechanics under the Companies Act, 2013 (verify section numbers against latest ICAI material): shares may be issued at par, at premium, or — for sweat equity only — at discount; Section 53 prohibits issue at a discount otherwise. Securities Premium may be used only for the specified purposes (bonus shares, writing off preliminary expenses, buy-back premium, etc.). Journal flow for issue: Bank A/c Dr / To Share Application A/c; on allotment, Share Application A/c Dr / To Share Capital A/c; calls follow the same debit/credit logic.

    • Forfeiture: debit Share Capital (called-up amount), credit Calls-in-Arrears and Forfeited Shares A/c; on re-issue, discount on re-issue cannot exceed the forfeited amount, and the balance transfers to Capital Reserve.
    • Debentures: issued like shares; discount/loss on issue is written off; redemption uses Debenture Redemption Reserve where applicable (verify current DRR requirements against latest ICAI material).
    • Buy-back: only out of free reserves, securities premium, or proceeds of a fresh issue; capped conditions apply under the Act (verify against latest ICAI material).

    Cash Flow Statement (AS 3)

    Classify every flow into Operating, Investing, or Financing activities. The indirect method starts from profit before tax and adjusts: add back non-cash charges (depreciation, provisions), add non-operating losses, subtract non-operating gains, then adjust for working-capital changes — increase in current assets is a cash outflow (subtract), increase in current liabilities is an inflow (add); finally subtract tax paid. Interest and dividend paid are financing activities; interest and dividend received are investing activities (for a non-financial enterprise). Traps: depreciation is added back because no cash left the business; profit on sale of machinery is deducted from operating profit and the full sale proceeds shown under investing.

    Mini-formats to memorise

    P&L Appropriation (skeleton): Net profit b/d → Less: Interest on capital → Less: Partner salaries/commission → = Divisible profit → distributed in PSR. If the deed is silent, skip straight to equal sharing — writing appropriations the deed does not allow is the classic mark-loser.

    Share issue at premium (journal flow): on application, Bank A/c Dr / To Share Application A/c; on allotment, Share Application A/c Dr / To Share Capital A/c (face value) / To Securities Premium A/c (premium). Calls in arrears are debited to a separate Calls-in-Arrears A/c, never netted off share capital.

    3. Business Laws (Contract Act, Sale of Goods, LLP, Companies Act 2013)

    Law answers score when they move from provision to facts in three steps: state the rule, cite the section, apply it. Memorise section numbers with their one-line rule — examiners reward precision. (Section numbers and limits below follow ICAI study material; verify against the latest ICAI material before the exam, as amendments can shift them.)

    The Indian Contract Act, 1872

    • Essentials of a valid contract (Sec. 10): lawful offer and acceptance, intention to create legal relations, lawful consideration, capacity of parties, free consent, lawful object, and not expressly declared void.
    • Offer vs invitation to offer: an advertisement or price list is an invitation; the customer's order is the offer. Acceptance (Sec. 2(b)) must be absolute, unqualified, and communicated — silence is not acceptance. The postal rule: acceptance is complete against the proposer when the letter is posted.
    • Consideration (Sec. 25): "something in return"; must be at the desire of the promisor and lawful. General rule: an agreement without consideration is void — exceptions include registered natural-love-and-affection agreements between near relatives, compensation for past voluntary services, and time-barred debt promises in writing.
    • Capacity (Sec. 11): a minor's agreement is void ab initio (Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose); necessaries supplied to a minor are payable from the minor's property.
    • Free consent (Sec. 14): vitiated by coercion (Sec. 15), undue influence (Sec. 16), fraud (Sec. 17), misrepresentation (Sec. 18), or mistake (Sec. 20–22). Coercion makes the contract voidable at the aggrieved party's option.
    • Contingent contracts (Sec. 31): performance depends on a collateral event; wagering agreements (Sec. 30) are void.
    • Quasi-contracts (Sec. 68–72): obligations resembling contracts — necessaries to incapable persons, money paid by an interested person, non-gratuitous acts, finder of goods, money paid by mistake.
    • Breach remedies: damages (Sec. 73 — ordinary and special, the latter only if contemplated), specific performance, injunction, rescission, and quantum meruit. Penalty vs liquidated damages: Indian courts grant only reasonable compensation (Sec. 74), even if the contract names a sum.

    The Sale of Goods Act, 1930

    • Condition vs warranty (Sec. 12): a condition is essential to the contract's main purpose — its breach allows rejection; a warranty is collateral — breach allows damages only.
    • Caveat emptor is the default, pierced by implied conditions: sale by description (Sec. 15), fitness for purpose (Sec. 16), merchantable quality, and sale by sample (Sec. 17).
    • Transfer of property: risk follows property (Sec. 26). For specific goods in deliverable state, property passes on contract (Sec. 20); for unascertained goods, on appropriation with assent (Sec. 23).
    • Unpaid seller's rights (Sec. 45–58): lien, stoppage in transit, right of resale, and suit for price/damages. A lien is lost when goods are delivered to a carrier without reservation.

    LLP Act, 2008 & Companies Act, 2013

    • LLP: body corporate with separate legal personality and perpetual succession; partners' liability is limited to their agreed contribution, and one partner's wrongful act does not bind others (unlike a firm). Minimum two designated partners, at least one resident in India.
    • Company formation: MOA (charter; defines objects and capital) and AOA (internal regulations) are the constitutional documents; incorporation creates a separate legal person (Salomon v. Salomon — verify case citations against ICAI material). Private companies restrict share transfer and cap members at 200; OPCs have a single member.
    • Meetings and governance: AGM within six months of financial-year end (verify current timelines against latest ICAI material); quorum, proxy, and voting rules in the Act; directors' duties and related-party restrictions are examinable favourites.

    Doctrines that decide case-study questions

    • Ultra vires: acts beyond the MOA's objects clause are void and cannot be ratified even unanimously — know this before attempting any "can the company do X" question.
    • Indoor management (Royal British Bank v. Turquand): outsiders may assume internal procedures were properly followed; the exception is when the outsider had knowledge of the irregularity or was put on inquiry.
    • Constructive notice: MOA and AOA are public documents — everyone dealing with the company is deemed to know their contents.
    • Lifting the corporate veil: courts ignore separate personality for fraud, tax evasion, or to identify the real controllers — the exception, not the rule.

    Trap sheet: "agreement" ≠ "contract" (a contract is an agreement enforceable by law, Sec. 2(h)); an invitation to offer is never an offer; a minor cannot ratify on attaining majority; wagering agreements are void, not illegal; in sale of goods, "property" means ownership, not the goods themselves.

    5. Business Economics (Micro & Macro)

    Business Economics splits into two halves: micro (how firms and consumers decide) and macro (how the whole economy behaves). The micro half is diagram-heavy; the macro half is definition-heavy. Master both vocabularies.

    Foundations: scarcity, choice, and the PPC

    • Central problems of an economy: what to produce, how to produce, and for whom — every system (market, planned, mixed) answers them differently.
    • Opportunity cost is the next-best alternative forgone — the single most tested definition in the paper. The Production Possibility Curve is concave to the origin because of increasing opportunity cost; points inside the curve mean unemployed resources, points outside are unattainable.
    • Positive vs normative: "what is" (testable) vs "what ought to be" (value judgement) — one-mark questions love this pair.

    Microeconomics

    • Demand: quantity demanded falls as price rises (law of demand) — exceptions: Giffen goods, Veblen/prestige goods, expectations of future price changes. Demand shifts when income, tastes, prices of related goods, or expectations change (movement along the curve is only from own-price changes).
    • Elasticity: price elasticity Ep = (%ΔQ)/(%ΔP). |Ep| > 1 elastic, < 1 inelastic, = 1 unitary. Revenue is maximised where |Ep| = 1. Income elasticity separates normal goods (positive) from inferior goods (negative); cross elasticity is positive for substitutes, negative for complements.
    • Supply: rises with price; shifts with input costs, technology, and taxes. Equilibrium is where demand meets supply — a price ceiling below equilibrium creates a shortage; a floor above it creates a surplus.
    • Production and costs: law of variable proportions — marginal product first rises, then diminishes (diminishing marginal returns). Short-run costs: AFC falls continuously, AVC and AC are U-shaped, MC cuts both at their minima. Long-run AC (the envelope curve) reflects economies then diseconomies of scale.
    • Market structures: perfect competition (P = MC, zero long-run economic profit), monopoly (MR = MC, P > MC, deadweight loss), monopolistic competition (differentiated products, excess capacity), oligopoly (few firms, kinked demand curve, collusion/cartel temptation). The exam loves asking which structure has which feature — make a comparison table while revising.

    Macroeconomics

    • National income: GDP = C + I + G + (X − M) (expenditure method); NNP = GNP − depreciation; personal and disposable income follow by subtracting taxes and adding transfers. Nominal GDP uses current prices, real GDP uses base-year prices — the GDP deflator = (Nominal/Real)·100.
    • Money: M1 (currency + demand deposits, narrow money), M3 (M1 + time deposits, broad money) — verify RBI's current monetary aggregate definitions against ICAI material. Money multiplier = 1/reserve ratio.
    • Inflation: measured by CPI (retail) and WPI (wholesale); demand-pull vs cost-push causes. Phillips curve: short-run trade-off between inflation and unemployment.
    • Fiscal policy: government spending and taxation — deficit concepts (revenue, fiscal, primary deficit) are classic one-mark questions. Monetary policy: RBI tools — repo rate, reverse repo, CRR, SLR, open market operations (verify current rates and framework against latest ICAI material; rates change).
    • Balance of payments: current account (trade in goods/services, income, transfers) + capital account (investment flows) = overall balance; a depreciating rupee helps exporters and hurts importers.
    • Business cycles: expansion, peak, contraction/recession, trough — fiscal stimulus in downturns, tightening in booms.

    Exam-favourite extras

    • Externalities and public goods: a negative externality (pollution) means social cost > private cost — the standard justification for corrective taxes; public goods are non-excludable and non-rival, which is why markets under-provide them.
    • Exchange-rate regimes: fixed (central bank defends a parity), floating (market-determined), managed float (RBI's approach — intervene to curb volatility, not to target a level). Devaluation is a policy act under fixed rates; depreciation is a market movement under floating rates.
    • Multiplier: an initial rise in spending circulates — the simple multiplier = 1/(1 − MPC) = 1/MPS; higher the marginal propensity to consume, stronger the multiplier.

    Trap sheet: a shift of the curve vs movement along it (change in determinants vs own price); elasticity uses percentage changes, not absolute; GDP counts final goods only — intermediate goods are excluded to avoid double counting; repo rate up ⟹ borrowing costlier ⟹ inflation-fighting stance.

    6. Income Tax: Heads of Income, Deductions & Computation Basics

    Income tax in India is charged on the total income of the previous year at the rates in force for the relevant assessment year. Every rupee of income must be slotted into one of the five heads of income (Sections 14–59), and each head has its own computation rules. The CA exam rewards a disciplined method: classify first, compute under each head, then aggregate, then deduct Chapter VI-A deductions, then apply rates.

    The five heads of income

    HeadSectionsKey points
    Salaries15–17Chargeable on due or receipt basis, whichever is earlier. Salary includes basic pay, allowances, perquisites. Standard deduction (flat amount — verify against latest ICAI material for the current figure and regime availability) and entertainment allowance/professional tax relief under Section 16. Perquisites valued under Rule 3; employer contribution to PF/superannuation above limits taxable.
    Income from House Property22–27Chargeable on the annual value of property (deemed ownership counts). Self-occupied property: nil annual value, but interest on housing loan deductible up to the statutory ceiling (verify against latest ICAI material). Let-out property: rent received/receivable less municipal taxes = gross annual value, less 30% standard deduction and interest on borrowed capital.
    Profits and Gains of Business or Profession (PGBP)28–44Net-profit-per-books is only the starting point. Add back disallowances (e.g., Section 37 personal expenditure, 40(a)(ia) TDS defaults, 40A(3) cash payments beyond limits) and claim further deductions (depreciation under Section 32 at block-of-assets rates — verify against latest ICAI material). Presumptive schemes: 44AD (business, 6%/8% of turnover), 44ADA (profession), 44AE (transport).
    Capital Gains45–55Transfer of a capital asset. Short-term vs long-term depends on holding period (verify against latest ICAI material — holding periods and rates have been amended in recent Finance Acts). Computation: full value of consideration less cost of acquisition, cost of improvement, and transfer expenses. Exemptions: 54 (residential house), 54EC (specified bonds), 54F (any long-term asset into residential house).
    Income from Other Sources56–59The residuary head: dividends, interest on securities, winnings from lotteries, gifts above the threshold (verify against latest ICAI material), family pension (1/3 or ceiling deduction).

    Clubbing, set-off and carry forward

    • Clubbing (Sections 60–65): income of spouse/minor child may be clubbed with the assessee's income in specified cases (e.g., transfer without adequate consideration, minor child's income except from own skill).
    • Set-off (Section 70–71): intra-head set-off first, then inter-head (with restrictions — e.g., capital losses only against capital gains; speculative losses only against speculative profits).
    • Carry forward (Sections 72–74A): business loss 8 years (return filed on time — Section 80), unabsorbed depreciation indefinitely (Section 32(2)), capital losses 8 years. Filing the return by the due date is the price of carry-forward — a favourite exam trap.

    Chapter VI-A deductions (from Gross Total Income)

    SectionScope
    80CLIC, PPF, ELSS, principal on housing loan etc. — aggregate ceiling verify against latest ICAI material
    80CCD(1B)Additional NPS contribution beyond 80C
    80DMedical insurance premium (higher limit for senior citizens)
    80TTA / 80TTBSavings-bank interest / senior-citizen interest income
    80EInterest on education loan — no ceiling, 8 years
    80GDonations (100%/50%, with/without qualifying limit)

    The computation ladder

    1. Compute income under each of the five heads.
    2. Apply clubbing, then intra-head and inter-head set-off → Gross Total Income (GTI).
    3. Less Chapter VI-A deductions → Total Income (rounded to nearest ₹10 under Section 288A).
    4. Apply slab rates or special rates (e.g., 115BB on winnings) → tax → add surcharge and Health & Education Cess (4%) → less TDS/TCS/advance tax → tax payable/refundable.

    Old vs new regime (Section 115BAC): the default new regime taxes at concessional slab rates but forgoes most deductions and exemptions; the old regime keeps them. Always compare both in exam problems. Slab rates, rebate thresholds and surcharge caps change almost every Finance Act — verify against latest ICAI material.

    Common traps: treating exempt income as taxable (Section 10 list — agricultural income, PPF interest etc.), forgetting the due-date condition for loss carry-forward, mixing up perquisite valuation rules, and applying new-regime deductions. Advance tax is payable in instalments (15/45/75/100%) when tax liability exceeds ₹10,000; Section 234B/234C interest punishes shortfall.

    7. GST: Levy, Input Tax Credit & Returns Basics

    Goods and Services Tax is a destination-based tax on the supply of goods or services, levied concurrently by the Centre and the States: CGST + SGST on intra-state supplies, IGST on inter-state supplies (and imports), UTGST in union territories without legislatures. Introduced by the 101st Constitutional Amendment (2016), GST subsumed excise, service tax, VAT, entry tax and a host of cesses into one framework.

    Levy and charge (Sections 7–9, CGST Act)

    • Taxable event: supply. Supply includes sale, transfer, barter, exchange, licence, rental, lease and disposal made for consideration in the course or furtherance of business. Schedule I deems certain supplies taxable even without consideration (e.g., stock transfers between distinct persons, gifts to employees beyond the threshold).
    • Reverse charge (Section 9(3)–(4)): specified supplies (e.g., GTA services, legal services to business entities) and purchases from unregistered dealers (in notified cases) shift the liability to the recipient — a staple MCQ area.
    • Composition scheme (Section 10): small suppliers pay a flat rate on turnover instead of normal GST and cannot collect tax or claim ITC. Turnover ceiling and rates are periodically revised — verify against latest ICAI material.

    Time, place and value of supply

    • Time of supply (Sections 14–15): for goods — earlier of invoice date or payment receipt date; for services — earlier of invoice or payment (with the 30/60-day invoice rules). Time of supply fixes which return period the tax belongs to.
    • Place of supply (IGST Act, Sections 10–13): determines whether a supply is intra-state (CGST+SGST) or inter-state (IGST). For goods: generally the location where movement terminates; for services: generally the recipient's location (B2B) or the supplier's (B2C), with special rules for immovable-property services, transport, and OIDAR services.
    • Value of supply (Section 15): the transaction value — price actually paid or payable — adjusted for discounts, subsidies linked to price, and amounts the supplier is liable to pay but recovered from the recipient. Valuation Rules apply where consideration is not wholly in money or parties are related.

    Input Tax Credit (Sections 16–18)

    ITC is the backbone of GST: tax paid on inputs is set off against output tax so that tax falls only on value added. Conditions (Section 16): the recipient must possess a tax invoice, have received the goods/services, have furnished the return, and the supplier must have paid the tax to the government.

    • Blocked credits (Section 17(5)): motor vehicles (with exceptions), food and beverages, outdoor catering, beauty treatment, health services, works contract services for immovable property, and personal-use goods/services — memorise this list; examiners love it.
    • Apportionment (Section 17(1)–(2)): where inputs serve both taxable and exempt supplies, or business and non-business purposes, ITC is restricted proportionately (Rule 42/43 formulas).
    • ITC on capital goods: available in full in the year of purchase (unlike the old staggered CENVAT), subject to the same conditions.

    Registration, returns and payment

    • Registration (Sections 22–25): mandatory above the aggregate-turnover threshold (verify against latest ICAI material — thresholds differ for goods vs services and special-category states), for inter-state suppliers, reverse-charge recipients, e-commerce operators and others regardless of turnover.
    • Returns: GSTR-1 (outward supplies, monthly/quarterly), GSTR-3B (summary return with payment, monthly), GSTR-9 (annual return above the threshold). E-invoicing under Rule 48(4) applies to businesses above the notified turnover — verify against latest ICAI material.
    • Payment: electronic cash ledger and credit ledger; ITC utilisation order (IGST → CGST → SGST per Section 49A/49B as amended).

    Common traps

    Confusing place-of-supply rules (they decide CGST+SGST vs IGST, not the rate); claiming ITC on blocked credits; forgetting the GSTR-2B matching discipline — ITC beyond what appears in auto-drafted statements invites scrutiny; and treating exempt, nil-rated and zero-rated supplies identically — zero-rated (exports, SEZ) allows ITC refund, exempt does not.

    8. Auditing: Standards, Evidence & Company Audit

    An audit is an independent examination of financial information to express an opinion on whether the financial statements give a true and fair view. Under the CA course, auditing rests on three pillars: the Standards on Auditing (SAs) issued by ICAI's AASB, the Companies Act, 2013 provisions on company audit, and the Code of Ethics governing chartered accountants.

    Key Standards on Auditing

    SASubjectExam essence
    SA 200Overall objectives of the independent auditorReasonable (not absolute) assurance; professional scepticism; professional judgement throughout.
    SA 210Agreeing the terms of audit engagementsEngagement letter; preconditions for an audit.
    SA 230Audit documentationWorking papers: sufficient, timely, retrievable; assembly within 60 days.
    SA 300Planning an auditAudit plan and strategy; planning is continuous, not a one-time step.
    SA 315Identifying and assessing risks of material misstatementUnderstand the entity and its environment, including internal control.
    SA 320MaterialityPerformance materiality < overall materiality; misstatements that could influence users' decisions.
    SA 500Audit evidenceEvidence must be sufficient (quantity) and appropriate (relevance + reliability).
    SA 501Specific considerations for selected itemsInventory (attendance at counts), litigation, segment information.
    SA 505External confirmationsDirect confirmations from debtors/banks — strong reliability.
    SA 520Analytical proceduresRatios and trends as substantive procedures and in overall review.
    SA 560Subsequent eventsEvents between balance-sheet date and report date requiring adjustment or disclosure.
    SA 570Going concernEvaluate management's assessment (at least 12 months); emphasis-of-matter or qualification if doubt.
    SA 700/701/705/706Forming an opinion; KAM; modifications; EOM/other matterUnmodified vs qualified vs adverse vs disclaimer; Key Audit Matters for listed entities.

    Audit evidence: techniques and reliability

    Procedures: inspection, observation, external confirmation, recalculation, reperformance, analytical procedures, and inquiry. Reliability hierarchy: external evidence beats internal; documentary beats oral; evidence obtained directly by the auditor beats evidence obtained indirectly. Inquiry alone is never sufficient — always corroborate. Sampling (SA 530): sampling risk vs non-sampling risk; larger samples where control risk is high.

    Internal control and vouching/verification

    Evaluate the control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information systems, and monitoring (the five COSO components in substance). Test of controls vs substantive procedures. Vouching = verifying the documentary evidence behind entries; verification = confirming existence, ownership and valuation of assets/liabilities — existence, rights and obligations, completeness, valuation, presentation assertions.

    Company audit under the Companies Act, 2013

    • Appointment (Section 139): first auditor by the Board within 30 days of incorporation (else members within 90 days via EGM); subsequent auditors appointed by members at each AGM for a 5-year term, ratification requirement removed by amendment.
    • Rotation (Section 139(2)): listed and prescribed classes of companies must rotate individual auditors every 5 years and audit firms every 10 years, with a 5-year cooling period — verify against latest ICAI material for the prescribed class thresholds.
    • Eligibility and disqualifications (Section 141): only a CA in practice; disqualified if the auditor (or relative/partner) holds securities beyond the limit, is indebted beyond the limit, has business relationships, or was an employee/officer in the preceding period.
    • Removal/resignation (Sections 140, 115): removal before term needs special resolution plus Central Government approval; resignation requires filing ADT-3 with reasons.
    • Duties and powers (Section 143): right of access to books, vouchers and explanations; duty to report fraud to the Central Government above the prescribed amount (report to the Board/Audit Committee below it); compliance with SAs mandatory (Section 143(9)–(10)).
    • Audit report (Section 143(3)): report on accounts examined, compliance with accounting standards, and the Companies (Auditor's Report) Order — CARO applicability and clause coverage (verify against latest ICAI material — CARO clauses are amended periodically).

    Ethics

    The CA Act, 1949 (Schedules I and II) defines professional misconduct — e.g., disclosing client information, soliciting work by advertisement (with defined exceptions), undercutting fees, or certifying without verification. The ICAI Code of Ethics rests on integrity, objectivity, professional competence and due care, confidentiality, and professional behaviour; threats (self-interest, self-review, advocacy, familiarity, intimidation) must be identified and safeguarded.

    Common traps: claiming absolute assurance; calling vouching and verification the same thing; forgetting the Board's 30-day window for the first auditor; applying rotation to every company; and treating a qualified opinion and an emphasis-of-matter paragraph as interchangeable — a qualification modifies the opinion, an EOM does not.

    9. Financial Management: Ratios, Leverage & Capital Budgeting

    Financial management is about three decisions: investment (where to put money), financing (how to raise it), and dividend (how much to return). The CA paper tests these through ratio analysis, leverage measurement, cost of capital, and capital budgeting — all formula-heavy, so learn each formula with its decision rule.

    Ratio analysis

    CategoryRatioFormulaReads as
    LiquidityCurrent ratioCurrent assets ÷ Current liabilitiesShort-term solvency; 2:1 is the conventional benchmark
    Quick (acid-test) ratio(Current assets − Inventory − Prepaid) ÷ Current liabilitiesStricter liquidity; 1:1 benchmark
    Cash ratioCash & equivalents ÷ Current liabilitiesImmediate paying capacity
    SolvencyDebt–equity ratioLong-term debt ÷ EquityFinancial risk; lower is safer
    Interest coverageEBIT ÷ InterestAbility to service debt
    ActivityInventory turnoverCOGS ÷ Average inventoryStock efficiency; convert to days: 365 ÷ turnover
    Receivables turnoverCredit sales ÷ Average receivablesCollection efficiency (days sales outstanding)
    ProfitabilityGross profit marginGross profit ÷ Sales × 100Pricing and production efficiency
    Net profit marginPAT ÷ Sales × 100Overall efficiency
    Return on capital employedEBIT ÷ Capital employed × 100Return on total long-term funds

    DuPont decomposition (ROE): ROE = (Net profit ÷ Sales) × (Sales ÷ Assets) × (Assets ÷ Equity) — margin × turnover × leverage. Examiners use it to diagnose whether a high ROE comes from operations or from borrowing.

    Leverage

    • Degree of Operating Leverage (DOL) = Contribution ÷ EBIT = %ΔEBIT ÷ %ΔSales. Measures business risk from fixed operating costs.
    • Degree of Financial Leverage (DFL) = EBIT ÷ EBT = %ΔEPS ÷ %ΔEBIT. Measures financial risk from fixed financial charges (interest).
    • Degree of Combined Leverage (DCL) = DOL × DFL = Contribution ÷ EBT = %ΔEPS ÷ %ΔSales. Total risk of the firm.
    • Financial break-even: the EBIT level at which EPS = 0, i.e., EBIT = Interest + Preference dividend ÷ (1 − t). Used in indifference-point problems comparing financing plans.

    Cost of capital

    Cost of equity (Ke): dividend-growth model Ke = (D1 ÷ P0) + g, or CAPM Ke = Rf + β(Rm − Rf). Cost of debt: Kd = I(1 − t) — interest is tax-deductible, so always use the after-tax cost. Cost of preference shares: Kp = D ÷ P0. WACC = Σ(weight × component cost), weights at market value. Decision rule: accept projects whose return exceeds WACC; WACC is the hurdle rate and the discount rate for NPV.

    Capital budgeting techniques

    MethodComputationDecision rule
    Payback periodInitial outlay ÷ Annual cash inflow (even flows)Shorter is better; ignores time value — a weakness to state explicitly
    Discounted paybackPayback using discounted cash flowsShorter is better; still ignores post-payback flows
    Accounting rate of return (ARR)Average PAT ÷ Average investment × 100Higher is better; uses accounting profit, not cash
    Net present value (NPV)PV of inflows − PV of outflows at the cost of capitalAccept if NPV > 0 — the theoretically superior method
    Internal rate of return (IRR)Discount rate at which NPV = 0Accept if IRR > cost of capital; beware multiple IRRs with non-conventional cash flows
    Profitability index (PI)PV of inflows ÷ PV of outflowsAccept if PI > 1; best for capital rationing rankings

    Cash flow discipline: use incremental after-tax cash flows, add back depreciation (non-cash), include working-capital changes and opportunity costs, exclude sunk costs. NPV and IRR can conflict on mutually exclusive projects with different scales or timing — NPV governs because it measures absolute wealth creation.

    Working capital (essentials)

    Operating cycle = Inventory days + Receivables days − Payables days. Permanent vs temporary working capital; the hedging (matching) approach vs conservative vs aggressive financing policies. EOQ = √(2AO ÷ C) for inventory ordering; cash management via the Baumol model. Receivables policy trades off credit sales growth against bad debts and collection cost.

    Common traps: using book values instead of market values in WACC; forgetting the (1 − t) on debt; applying ARR to cash flows or payback to discounted flows; ranking mutually exclusive projects by IRR instead of NPV; and ignoring working-capital release in the terminal year of a project.

    10. Business Correspondence, Ethics & Communication

    This area (CA Foundation Paper 2, Section B — Business Correspondence and Reporting) tests whether you can communicate like a professional: draft precisely, structure documents correctly, and act ethically. Marks come from format discipline and formal register, not vocabulary display.

    The communication process

    Sender → encoding → message → channel → decoding → receiver → feedback, with noise at every stage. Types: verbal (oral/written), non-verbal (body language, paralanguage, proxemics, chronemics), formal (follows the chain of command — upward, downward, horizontal) and informal/grapevine (fast, but prone to distortion). Barriers: semantic (jargon, ambiguous words), psychological (prejudice, inattention), organisational (hierarchy, information overload), physical (distance, faulty channels), and cultural. Overcoming them: clarity, active listening, feedback loops, appropriate channel choice, and empathy.

    Drafting formats examiners expect

    • Formal letters: sender's address, date, receiver's address, subject line, salutation (Dear Sir/Madam), body (introduction–purpose–detail–action), complimentary close (Yours faithfully), signature block with designation. Types: enquiry, quotation, order, complaint, adjustment, collection, circular.
    • Memos (inter-office memoranda): To / From / Date / Subject headers, no salutation or close, concise and directive — used for internal communication, policy announcements, and meeting notices.
    • Emails: precise subject line, formal greeting, short paragraphs, clear call to action, professional sign-off; CC vs BCC etiquette — never expose client addresses in mass mailings.
    • Notices, agendas and minutes: notice carries date, time, venue and agenda; minutes record decisions and action items in past tense, confirmed at the next meeting.
    • Reports: title page, terms of reference, findings, conclusions, recommendations — in the order the reader needs them; executive summary first for decision-makers.
    • Précis writing: one-third the length of the original, in your own words, preserving all essential points and the original tone — no examples, no commentary, usually a single paragraph flow with a title.

    Comprehension and note-taking

    Read questions before the passage; distinguish fact from opinion and main idea from supporting detail. Notes use headings, abbreviations and logical sequencing — they are a tool for recall, not a second copy of the text. In answers, prefer active voice, short sentences, and one idea per paragraph.

    Business ethics

    • Core principles: integrity, objectivity, professional competence and due care, confidentiality, professional behaviour — the same pillars as the ICAI Code of Ethics, applied to business conduct generally.
    • Ethical threats: self-interest, self-review, advocacy, familiarity, intimidation — identify the threat, then apply safeguards (disclosure, consultation, withdrawal).
    • Corporate governance: the board's accountability to stakeholders; independent directors, audit committees, and transparent disclosure as safeguards against agency problems.
    • CSR (Section 135, Companies Act): prescribed companies must spend on Schedule VII activities and report it — verify against latest ICAI material for applicability thresholds.
    • Whistle-blowing and ethical dilemmas: frameworks — legality test, publicity test, stakeholder test. In exam case studies, recommend the course that protects the public interest and complies with the law, and state the reasoning explicitly.

    Workplace communication skills

    Meetings: agenda in advance, time-boxed discussion, recorded action items with owners. Presentations: audience analysis, rule of three for structure (tell them what you'll say, say it, tell them what you said), visual aids as support not script. Negotiation: separate people from the problem, focus on interests not positions, generate options before deciding. Interviews (as candidate or panel): preparation, structured questions, documented evaluation criteria.

    Sentence-level craft: define technical terms on first use, keep one idea per sentence, and match the document's register to its audience — a board report tolerates jargon a client letter must explain. Avoid redundancy ("advance planning", "end result"), prefer concrete verbs over nominalisations ("we recommend" beats "a recommendation is made"), and proofread for agreement errors, which examiners penalise in drafting questions.

    Common traps: informal register in formal drafts (contractions, slang); missing format elements (subject line, designation in signature); précis that copies sentences instead of condensing ideas; ethics answers that moralise instead of applying the threat-and-safeguard framework; and confusing minutes (record of what was decided) with reports (analysis with recommendations).

    11. Accounting Standards: AS-1 to AS-29 Exam Map

    Accounting Standards are the favourite theory-plus-application area of CA Foundation Paper 1 (Accounting) and return in harder form at Inter (AS and Ind AS). Examiners test three things: which standard governs a situation, the core recognition or measurement rule, and the mandatory disclosures. Learn the standards as a map, not as isolated paragraphs — each standard answers one question: when do we recognize an item, how do we measure it, and what must we disclose.

    The framework standards: AS-1, AS-5, AS-29

    AS-1 (Disclosure of Accounting Policies) names three fundamental accounting assumptions — going concern, consistency and accrual. If they are followed, no disclosure is needed; if any is not followed, the fact must be disclosed. AS-5 (Net Profit or Loss, Prior Period Items and Changes in Accounting Policies) separates ordinary activities from extraordinary items and prior period items, and insists that a change in accounting policy be made only when required by statute, by a standard, or for better presentation — with the effect disclosed. AS-29 (Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets) is the gatekeeper of prudence: a provision is recognized only when there is a present obligation from a past event, a probable outflow, and a reliable estimate. Contingent liabilities are disclosed (never recognized) unless the outflow is remote; contingent assets are never recognized and are disclosed only when the inflow is probable.

    Asset standards: AS-2, AS-6, AS-10, AS-13, AS-26

    AS-2 (Inventories) measures stock at the lower of cost and net realizable value, with cost on FIFO or weighted average; abnormal wastage, storage (unless production needs it) and selling costs are excluded. AS-10 (Property, Plant and Equipment) capitalizes self-constructed assets at direct cost plus attributable overheads, and capitalizes later spending only when it improves the asset beyond its originally assessed performance. AS-6 (Depreciation Accounting) requires disclosure of the depreciable amount, useful life and method for each class of asset. AS-13 (Investments) carries current investments at the lower of cost and fair value (per investment or per category) and long-term investments at cost less any other-than-temporary decline. AS-26 (Intangible Assets) draws the famous line: research is always expensed, while development is capitalized only on demonstrated technical feasibility, intent, ability and probable future benefits — with amortization over useful life subject to a rebuttable ten-year presumption.

    Liability, income and special standards: AS-4, AS-7, AS-9, AS-11, AS-12, AS-15, AS-16, AS-18, AS-19, AS-20, AS-22

    AS-4 (Contingencies and Events after the Balance Sheet Date): adjusting events (evidence of conditions existing at the year-end, like a litigation settlement) change the numbers; non-adjusting events (a post-year-end fire) are only disclosed — and dividends proposed after the year-end are not recognized as a liability. AS-9 (Revenue Recognition) recognizes sale revenue when risks and rewards pass and collection is reasonably certain. AS-12 (Government Grants) presents asset-related grants as deferred income or as a deduction from the asset, and treats refundable grants as extraordinary items. AS-16 (Borrowing Costs) capitalizes interest on qualifying assets (those needing substantial time) and suspends capitalization during extended interruptions. AS-19 (Leases) classifies by substance: finance leases transfer substantially all risks and rewards and go on the balance sheet at the lower of fair value and present value of minimum payments; operating lease rentals are expensed straight-line. AS-20 (EPS) divides profit attributable to equity shareholders by weighted average shares, restating prior periods for bonus issues. AS-22 (Taxes on Income) creates deferred tax only on timing differences, recognizing deferred tax assets only with reasonable certainty. AS-18 (Related Party Disclosures) presumes significant influence at 20% voting power and demands disclosure of relationships, transactions and balances.

    How to score

    • Anchor every standard to one trigger phrase: AS-2 = lower of cost or NRV; AS-16 = qualifying asset; AS-19 = risks and rewards; AS-29 = present obligation + probable + measurable.
    • In case studies, first name the standard, then apply its recognition rule, then state the disclosure — examiners award stepwise marks.
    • Watch the classic traps: proposed dividend under revised AS-4 (disclose, do not provide); research vs development under AS-26; contingent liability vs provision under AS-29.
    • Disclosure requirements are the easiest marks in the paper — revise the disclosure list of each standard separately in the last week.

    12. Cost & Management Accounting: Inter/Final Bridge

    Cost accounting begins where financial accounting ends: financial accounts tell you the profit; cost accounts tell you why — which product, department or activity earned it. This chapter bridges Foundation costing basics to the CA Intermediate Cost and Management Accounting paper. The entire subject rests on one discipline: classifying every rupee of cost correctly, then choosing the right technique for the decision at hand.

    Cost classification — the foundation of everything

    Costs are classified by nature (material, labour, expenses), by function (production, administration, selling and distribution), by behaviour (fixed, variable, semi-variable), and by traceability (direct vs indirect). Direct costs are traced to a cost object; indirect costs (overheads) are apportioned and then absorbed, usually on a base like labour hours or machine hours. The exam favourite is behaviour: fixed costs stay constant in total within the relevant range, variable costs move in direct proportion to output, and semi-variable costs (like a telephone bill with a fixed rental plus call charges) have both elements. Marginal costing treats only variable costs as product costs and writes off fixed costs as period costs; absorption costing charges both to the product — so the two methods report different profits whenever inventory levels change.

    Material, labour and overhead control

    Material: reorder level = maximum consumption x maximum reorder period; minimum level = reorder level - (normal consumption x normal reorder period); EOQ = sqrt(2 x annual demand x ordering cost / carrying cost per unit). Pricing of issues uses FIFO, LIFO or weighted average — in rising prices FIFO gives higher profit and higher closing stock. Labour: time rate pays for attendance, piece rate pays for output; incentive plans (Halsey, Rowan, Taylor's differential, Merrick) share the gains of efficiency between worker and employer. Idle time and overtime premium need careful treatment — normal idle time is charged to the job or overhead, abnormal idle time goes to costing profit and loss. Overheads: allocation (whole item to one department), apportionment (shared items split on a logical base) and absorption (recovery through a rate) — under- or over-absorption is carried to costing profit and loss.

    Decision tools: CVP, budgets and standard costing

    Cost-Volume-Profit analysis runs on contribution: Contribution = Sales - Variable cost; P/V ratio = Contribution / Sales; break-even point (units) = Fixed cost / Contribution per unit; break-even sales = Fixed cost / P/V ratio; margin of safety = actual sales - break-even sales. Budgetary control compares actuals with budgets: flexible budgets adjust for activity levels, cash budgets track liquidity, and zero-based budgeting justifies every rupee from scratch. Standard costing sets predetermined costs and analyses variances: material price variance = (standard price - actual price) x actual quantity; material usage variance = (standard quantity - actual quantity) x standard price; labour rate and efficiency variances follow the same logic; overhead variances split into expenditure and volume. Variances are the management signals — adverse price variance with favourable usage variance, for example, hints at cheaper but wasteful material.

    How to score

    • Never start a numerical without writing the classification or formula first — method marks survive arithmetic slips.
    • Draw the cost sheet format from memory: prime cost, works cost, cost of production, cost of goods sold, cost of sales — in that order, every time.
    • In CVP questions, compute contribution per unit before anything else; most follow-up requirements fall out of it.
    • For variances, keep the mnemonic: price/rate variances use actual quantity, usage/efficiency variances use standard price — and always label favourable or adverse.
